planting.note: Direct sow after last frost near a trellis or tall support in full sun; Tarbais is a semi-vining pole-type bean traditionally grown up corn stalks in southwestern France and is best harvested dry for the classic cassoulet preparation, though it can be eaten as a fresh shell bean earlier in the season.

directions: Sow after last frost near a trellis, fence, or tall pole in full sun; Tarbais is the classic French heirloom bean of Gascon cuisine, historically grown climbing up corn stalks in the countryside around Tarbes in southwestern France, and it is the traditional bean specified in authentic cassoulet, the slow-cooked white bean and meat casserole of the region. The dry beans are creamy white, thin-skinned, and known for cooking up exceptionally tender and creamy while holding their shape, absorbing the rich flavors of the pork, duck, and sausage traditionally simmered with them in cassoulet. While best known dried, pods can also be picked earlier at the plump green shell-bean stage for a more delicate fresh bean dish. Let pods mature and dry fully on the vine for the classic dry-bean harvest, picking before fall rains can cause mold, and finish drying indoors in a well-ventilated spot before shelling and storing.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Covey (sold as Lavender Twist) is a weeping, cascading redbud that is typically grafted onto a standard trunk and needs its central leader staked while young to establish height before the weeping habit takes over.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Covey, marketed as Lavender Twist, is a distinctive weeping redbud cultivar with strongly cascading, contorted branches that arch and twist downward to create a dense, umbrella-like curtain of growth, completely unlike the upright vase shape of standard redbuds. In early spring, before the heart-shaped leaves emerge, the weeping branches are covered top to bottom in the same rosy-lavender pea-family flowers typical of redbud, creating a striking waterfall effect. Because it is usually grafted onto an upright standard trunk, young trees need a stake to help the leader gain height before the weeping side branches are allowed to cascade freely; without staking, the tree can sprawl low to the ground. It stays considerably smaller and more compact than a standard redbud, making it an excellent specimen for a small garden, courtyard, or as a dramatic focal point near a patio. Like other redbuds, it tolerates partial shade well and needs well-drained soil, since the roots are prone to rot in poorly drained sites.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Appalachian Red is grown for its unusually vivid magenta-red spring flower color, a distinct break from the softer pink-lavender of the straight species.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Appalachian Red is a North Carolina State University introduction selected for exceptionally vivid, deep magenta-red flowers that bloom on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, standing out sharply from the softer pink-lavender tones of the wild species and from the more common purple-leafed and pink-flowered cultivars already popular in the nursery trade. Green, heart-shaped summer foliage and a classic small-tree vase shape follow the spring flower display, with attractive yellow fall color. Like other redbuds it is a valuable, adaptable native flowering tree for the understory or edge of a woodland garden, tolerating a good range of soil types as long as drainage is adequate, since redbud roots are susceptible to rot in wet, poorly drained sites. It performs well as a specimen tree, in a mixed native shrub-and-tree border, or naturalized at a woodland edge where its striking bloom color provides one of the most vivid early-spring accents in a partly shaded Southern garden.
sources: North Carolina State University — Redbud Cultivar Introductions

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba is the standard white-flowered form of eastern redbud, a naturally occurring color variant of the straight species.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba is the classic white-flowered form of eastern redbud, a naturally occurring color break from the typical rosy-pink to lavender bloom of the wild species, covering bare branches in clean white pea-family flowers in early spring before the heart-shaped green leaves emerge. It provides a softer, more understated spring display than pink or magenta redbud cultivars and pairs especially well with purple-leafed selections like Forest Pansy planted nearby for contrast. Growth habit, size, and cultural needs match the straight species — a small, adaptable native tree well suited to the dappled light of a woodland edge or understory planting, tolerating partial shade better than many flowering trees, though bloom is most abundant with several hours of direct sun. As with all redbuds, plant in well-drained soil, since the roots are prone to rot in heavy, wet sites, and avoid disturbing the root system once established, since redbud transplants best when young and container-grown.

planting.note: Sow after last frost when soil has reached at least 60°F; Envy is one of the earliest-maturing edamame cultivars available and tolerates cooler soil at planting better than many other edamame varieties, allowing an earlier sowing date in spring.

directions: Sow seed 1 to 1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart in full sun; inoculate with soybean-specific rhizobium inoculant for best nitrogen fixation. Envy is a widely grown edamame cultivar valued for its notably early maturity — among the fastest edamame varieties to reach harvest — and for better cold-soil tolerance at planting than many other edamame types, making it a good choice for gardeners wanting the earliest possible edamame crop or a second planting for fall harvest. Plants are compact and productive, with pods clustering densely on relatively short, sturdy bushes. Harvest when pods are bright green, plump, and fully filled but before the shell begins to yellow — sample a pod for tenderness and flavor to judge exact timing. For the classic preparation, boil or steam whole pods briefly in well-salted water, then squeeze the beans directly from the pod to eat; pods themselves are fibrous and not eaten.

common_name: Excelsior Hybrid Foxglove (Classic Outward-Facing Mixed-Color Strain)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors or sow directly in late summer for fall transplanting; in zone 9 foxglove is grown as a winter annual or biennial, with plants established in fall blooming the following spring. Excelsior is the classic older foxglove strain, distinguished by densely packed, outward- and upward-facing florets held all the way around the spike rather than hanging to one side.

directions: Plant in partial shade — filtered light under tall trees suits it well — in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil; Excelsior Hybrids is the long-standing classic foxglove seed strain, bred to hold its tubular, spotted flowers evenly all the way around the spike in an outward- and upward-facing arrangement rather than the one-sided, downward-hanging habit of the older wild-type foxglove, giving a fuller, more dramatic bloom spike viewed from any angle. Flowers come in a mix of purple, pink, cream, and white, each with distinctive dark spotting inside the throat that guides pollinating bumblebees to the nectar. As a true biennial, plants form a low rosette of foliage in year one and send up the tall flowering spike in year two, though fall-sown plants in mild-winter zones can bloom the following spring; it self-seeds readily where happy, so a planting can sustain itself with new rosettes appearing each year once established. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where children or pets might sample the foliage or flowers, and wear gloves when handling.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost for bloom the same year; Foxy was one of the first foxglove strains bred to reliably flower from seed in a single season rather than requiring the traditional two-year biennial cycle.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil; Foxy was an All-America Selections award-winning foxglove strain notable as one of the earliest cultivars bred to reliably bloom the first year from an early indoor sowing, freeing gardeners from the traditional two-year wait required by standard biennial foxglove. It is more compact than older strains, typically topping out around 2.5–3.5 feet, with well-filled spikes of the classic spotted, tubular, bell-shaped flowers in a mix of purple, pink, and white. Start seed early indoors under lights for the best chance of first-season bloom, since a late start pushes flowering into the following year instead. In mild-winter gardens, plants may persist and rebloom as short-lived perennials or self-seed to naturalize a colony over a few seasons. All parts of Digitalis purpurea are toxic if ingested, so plant away from areas frequented by children or pets, and wear gloves when handling the foliage.
